84.t: Best clarinetist in town after Bechet
84.s: Who was considered best clarinetist; Handy came after Bechet left, then switched to alto and George Lewis rose.
84.q: No. They called him by his regular name. Yeah. Mm-hmm.

84.t: Other local clarinet players he heard
84.s: Interviewers ask about other clarinetists near Pass Christian; Handy says none was a real inspiration.
84.q: No, yeah, well, I heard something like that. Some of it was never, you know, outstanding clarinet player. He played a lot about music.

84.t: Best clarinetists in New Orleans; Piku and Robichaux's band
84.s: He names Joe Watson and others as best players and discusses Piku's reading and jazz playing.
84.q: Well, no, that's kind of a whole dance. That's a loaded question. Yeah, because I still like Joe Watson to my idea. Then there was Zell, he was with Redhead, yeah, he was with Redhead, he was supposed to beat him. Oh, yeah. Then there was Piku, Teo, all those guys, man.

84.s: Handy names Louis Cottrell and others, and describes Manuel Crusto, his many instruments and his drinking.
84.q: But they got, uh, some clarinet players around here that you know are here so often. Great. You take the president of our local, Louis Contrero. Mm-hmm. Great clarinet player. Great. You know, he'll, you know, hear much of him. But he's a great clarinet player. I only got another boy around here…

84.t: Favorite clarinet players: Joe Watson, Zib, Blind Freddy
84.s: Handy names the clarinetists he admired in New Orleans and a reading man who played only with Piron's band and never sat in.
84.ch: New Orleans clarinetists and Steve Lewis
84.q: I liked it, him for clarinet. Mm-hmm. And then I had another fellow, I liked it pretty good, played with Rene, called him Zib. Oh, yeah. Yeah, he was a nice clarinet player. Mm-hmm. And then I had this fellow, Blind Freddy. Mm-hmm. Wonderful. He could play about as much clarinet with one piece of…

84.t: Clarinetists Zeb and Watson; the band at Pete Herman's
84.s: Handy praises the clarinetists Zeb and Watson, then lists the band he had at Pete Herman's with Ridgely, Shots and Emma Barrett.
84.q: No, Zeb's dead. The guy I really liked to hear play clarinet. He played such a sweet clarinet. It was, uh, a fellow by the name of Watson. Used to play with Sam Morgan. I used to like to hear him play clarinet. And he used to like to hear me play. Because the OAC, he wanted me to blow. And I, you…

84.t: George Lewis and Willie Humphrey in the 1920s
84.s: George Lewis's rise around 1922, the after-hours jam spot, his unchanged style, and Willie Humphrey following.
84.q: Well, George started coming in the eye of the public around, I'd say around 22. Mm-hmm. In 1922. Because we was playing at, uh, at, uh, Humming Booth, at, uh, Elite. And when we'd get through there, I had a place back, Iberville Street, that, Iberville and Mariette called, uh, the Boothwa. Uh, all…

84.t: Sonny Johnson, a quiet great alto and clarinet player
84.s: Handy describes a reluctant, quiet musician, great on alto and clarinet, who once taught.
84.q: And he's a very quiet guy. He don't say nothing to nobody. He said that. And I bet he'd sit up there and play all night and wouldn't say three words. Never say nothing. Unless you ask him something. You ask him something. He'd give you that flat answer then. That's all. No more talk. He's a…

84.t: Clarinet players Sidney Bechet and Green, and Baton Rouge musicians
84.s: He wished to play against Bechet, recalls Green in Baton Rouge, and Titten Knox's strictly musical band.
84.q: Well that was all that was playing around here at that time. I didn't give up clarinet. When I wanted to, one man I wanted to meet with clarinet was Sidney Bessier. Uh huh. But I never got a chance to play against Sidney because he was in New York. He left a week before I come here. I never got a…

198.t: Lil Pills, Zeb and Blind Charlie: the lesser-known clarinetists
198.s: Barnes recalls the clarinetists who played with Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly, how they played, and what they looked like and where they came from.
198.q: Well, I'll tell you something about that. The clarinet players that played with, well, I remember Lil Pills. That was the only name I knew anymore. Now they had another one that was the clarinet players that was the clarinet players that was the clarinet players. Now, the clarinet players that was…

198.t: Big Eye Louis as favorite clarinetist: tone, originality, reading
198.s: Barnes says he got the chorus from Big Eye Louis and ranks him over Piku and others for tone and originality; Louis was a speller rather than a reader.
198.q: Later years. But the force would come now. Now you see, I learned from Piku, George. But my ideas were from Lloyd. Now Big R. Louis was a man that played a clarinet. And he could take a clarinet and make a rooster, curl, dog bark, anything like that. And that's why I learned he told him that…

198.t: George Baquet's fiery, loud clarinet playing
198.s: Asked about George Baquet's Buffet clarinet and style, Barnes calls him a fiery, very loud player.
198.q: that you can tell us something about it well george bakke was a was a kind of player that was fiery he done he made everything he's very fiery that's what i like loud loud loud loud loud very loud when you say

198.t: Georgia Boy and the high tone of the old clarinetists
198.s: Georgia Boy, who went with Pudgy, is remembered as a good player lost young; the clarinetists played high.
198.q: He played on all of them. He was a big sport. He gathered himself away, in other words, because he was well-knowing and well-liking. So, George, I was sorry. See him, he wasn't in TB. He wasn't in TB and we lost him.

198.s: Walter Barnes of Natchez was a good clarinetist who died in a fire; George Baquet was a sweet player and parade man, while Big Eye Louis was the real band man.
198.q: Did he play around New Orleans much? All those fellas, they didn't see him. They come on down here. We went on up there.

198.t: Strong clarinetists: Pills, Jimbo and George Lewis
198.s: He liked Pills, found Jimbo timid, does not remember George Lewis from then, and notes the men who left town.
198.q: Well George, George was alright. George Lewis was alright. But I didn't know George in, let's see. I was up in there in that time doing Jimbo. Doing Jimbo and Zep and them. I don't remember George at all.

198.t: How good Picou and his contemporaries were
198.s: Barnes says it was hard to choose among Picou, Baquet and the other clarinetists, all solid men.
198.ch: Zue Robertson, Bakke family and teachers
198.q: Well, during that time, it was hard to tell between Rocky, and Pico, and TU, and Charlie. Charlie and the Curtis. Yeah, it was hard to tell, because all those men was good. You know, now maybe it comes to a test, we could find it out. Yeah. I know in them days it was good. Because Pico was good,…

198.t: Big Eye Louis's swing style and Barnes's favorite clarinetist
198.s: Barnes says Big Eye Louis was a swinging improviser who always came back to the tune, and names him his favorite clarinetist.
198.ch: Big Eye Louis and Barnes's own playing
198.q: Oh, Big Eye Louie was a swing kind of player. And in the swing he had it. He had it, because what he'd do like I'd do. He'd make so much. You see, he'd make it, he'd just start a whole lot of foolishness. And he'd make it. And many men would make things, but they'd make it right. You know, like…

198.t: Clarinetists of the 1920s and Georgie Boyd
198.s: Barnes lists clarinet players in town in the 1920s including Jimbo, Johnny Dots, Pills, Zeb and Joe Watson, and calls George Boyd rougher than himself.
198.q: Well I don't know. In the 20s I believe we had Art and Hale. Here we had Jimbo. Yeah Jimbo was out here in the 20s. Now here we had Johnny Hunnicall. Johnny Dots. Johnny Dots. We had Pills. And uh. Had this other boy Zeb. Had Zeb. Then this boy Joe Watson. Had him. And uh. Kaiser. We had Kaiser. We…

724.t: Favorite clarinetists: Noone, Dodds, Tio and Big Eye
724.s: He names Jimmy Noone, Johnny Dodds, Lorenzo Tio and Big Eye as favorites and praises Tio's clean playing.
724.q: He played so clean. Mm-hmm. He played so clean. And he said clean, like each note would be cut cut off. Yeah, you know, no fumble. Yeah. I wish I'd heard him.

724.t: Clarinetist George Baquet's tone and a job with Punch Miller
724.s: He describes a big-toned clarinetist and plays one advertising job with Punch.
724.q: Well I guess I only had the opportunity to play one job with him and that was an advertisement. On the truck. On the truck. Yes.

724.t: Bob Lyons and Perez, and playing loud
724.s: A few jobs with Lyons, a Saturday job with Perez, and whether he was louder than other clarinetists.
724.q: Yeah, that's right. I want to ask you about Bob Lyons too. He had a band? Yeah, he had a band. You play with him much? Well, I played with him a little. Not long. But not with his group that he had when he hadn't been in. I don't know what had happened, but he just got a line up together. Little…

724.t: Nicknames like King and Kid, and playing in funerals as the clarinet wizard
724.s: Few clarinetists took titles; he recalls a parade with two clarinets in different keys.
724.q: The only one that called himself Kit was Wayne Smolga. Yeah. At least he had a sense of humor. Well, like, Kid Ari is a trauma-in-law, doesn't it? Kid Avery, Joe Avery. And Kid Williams, A. Well, anyway. But I never can recall a clarinet play doing that except for the moment of all. Kid Ernest.…

1.t: Big-Eye Louis, Picou and other New Orleans clarinetists
1.s: Danny describes Big-Eye Louis Nelson and Picou as masters of improvised clarinet and he and Milt try to recall an island clarinetist.
1.ch: Wagon bands, halls and the old brass bands
1.q: Big-Eye Louis [Nelson] was a great clarinet player, who was somewhat of a rival of Tio. Big-Eye Louis and Picou, they were masters of that style of playing, that improvisation...

1.t: Thornton Blue, the St. Louis clarinetist who challenged Buster Bailey
1.s: Thornton Blue hounded Buster Bailey until Bailey let him play, and he was a virtuoso whose father led the Imperial Band.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: So Buster said finally, "Go get your horn," and they went in the joint and they blew it all night. And Blue was a virtuoso. He'd come out of St. Louis. His father had the Imperial Band. I hung out with him a while. He told me a lot...

1.s: He names Willie Humphrey and other clarinetists he heard and worked with.
1.q: The one that impressed me most was Willie Humphrey. I saw him in the street parades, when I had a little E flat. You have the piercing sound over those brass bands, you know, really wailing on the horn.

1.t: Clarinetists George Boyd and George Lewis, playing in tune
1.s: Barker remembers George Boyd, stresses intonation on clarinet, and disparages the New Orleans standing of George Lewis's band.
1.ch: Second session: family, Armstrong and David Jones
1.q: No. They all had that sound of bending notes, playing the blues and all, but they all played in tune. They never deviated from playing some other notes or bending a note wrong. They played within the context of the music. That’s what’s got to be watched when you’re playing a clarinet. You got to…

37.t: Fazola's influence and the Bobcats clarinetists
37.s: Jug Burger reflects Fazola; Fazola is revered among Detroit-area Bobcats fans, while Eddie Miller is admired for tenor rather than clarinet.
37.q: Yeah. The name Jug Burger springs to mind. Uh-huh. Uh... Jug was very fond of... What was his nickname? Foz? Yes. And, uh... And Jug, I believe, is from New Orleans, or from Biloxi, or that neck of the woods. And he was very... Very fond of Foz. And his playing does reflect Foz's playing. But... I…

37.t: Matlock and Bob McCracken as accomplished but non-influential clarinetists
37.s: Chace sees no Chicago influence from Matlock or McCracken, from whom he bought his first clarinet, calling them competent players without personality.
37.q: Perhaps, but I'm simply not competent to say. It's almost 25 years since that time, isn't it? Yes. And I don't hear any talk about Matlock among different clarinet players. He's, of course, he's now one of the chieftains of the L.A. School of Playing, and everybody admires his work, but in…

37.t: No current New Orleans influence on Chicago players; Ray Burke and Fountain
37.s: Chace can name no New Orleans player copied locally, and sees no influence of Pete Fountain on anyone.
37.q: By... By... People you know around town. No. Certainly not directly. I can't think of anybody. Uh... You know... I can't think of playing, but it's awfully hard to tell. Uh...

37.t: Teschemacher and Pee Wee as founders of Chicago clarinet style
37.s: They agree Teschemacher and Pee Wee Russell underlie Chicago clarinet, with Rod Cless and Bud Jacobson as representatives.
37.ch: Teschemacher, Pee Wee, Noon and Simeon
37.q: It's my assumption, yes. The actual historical business is vague to me. I don't know exactly when or how often Pee-wee played in Chicago, but you can't discuss Chicago style without discussing Pee-wee's playing, I don't think.

571.t: New Orleans clarinetists who impressed Lewis
571.s: Lewis lists clarinetists he admired in New Orleans, including Charlie McCurtis, Picou, Baquet, Tio and George Boyd, and says each had a style of his own.
571.q: But I tell you, I was a lot of them. But, uh, every one of them made an impression on me because, excuse me, every one had their own style. I was, uh, Charlie McQuirtis, P. Kool-Eddie's Betts, George Bakke, uh, Lorenzo Teal, uh, Johnny, uh, Johnny Brown, and so many others. Zeb, uh, uh, Eddie…

571.t: Early clarinet favorites heard in the street
571.s: George says he thought all street clarinetists were good, naming George Baquet, Charlie McCurdy and Big Eye Louis.
571.q: Well Bill, I tell you, in my early days I thought they all were good, those I heard on the street. I know they all couldn't have been as good as I thought they were, but I heard a man like George Bakke, also Charlie McCurtis, T.O. and there was Big I, Louis. Big I, Louis.

571.t: Clarinet and trumpet players with a good tone
571.s: Lewis names players with fine tone, including Noone and Charlie McCurtis, and compares Fritz's tone to Edmund Hall's.
571.q: Uh... Charlie Bockey had a wonderful tone. Uh... Those were really professional men. Uh... Uh... Those were dear We called Pitman. Pitman? Yeah, Pitman, you know, Waterville.

571.t: Reading music in Mandeville bands; Zeb, Edmund Hall and clarinet tone
571.s: George says few bands there used music, names the clarinetist Zeb, and compares clarinet tones with Edmund Hall and Georgie Boyd.
571.ch: Mandeville, Bunk Johnson and society banquets
571.q: I never saw any music. I never saw no band use any music except, the first band I saw use music over there was Leonard Parker's band. And then Parker was a good spell a little bit and he used to, I saw him with music. But the rest of them I never saw anyone with no music. And then also René used to…

619.t: Lorenzo Tio as the greatest clarinetist
619.s: Laurent says no clarinetist could be greater than Lorenzo, who excelled at jazz, opera and brass band, playing E flat on parade.
619.q: Well I'm going to tell you at the time, at my time when I was talking about, I don't think it would come any greater than that boy Lorenzo. I don't think it would come any greater. I don't think it could come

619.t: George Baquet explains the flute-part variation
619.s: At the meeting records were played, Baquet did not recognise himself, and he said the variation came from a flute part transposed for clarinet, not from Picou.
619.q: He was a great drummer also. In them brass bands. Oh, he was a great drummer. We went to that meeting. We went to that meeting. Papa Celestine was there. So they began playing records. Disgusting numbers. They played just certain numbers. And they asked George Bakke. Say, can you tell me who was…

619.t: McCurdy, Picou and the flute-part story told again
619.s: Asked about McCurdy, Laurent repeats the Baquet account, set on an out-of-town job, and recalls playing duets with Picou in a backyard.
619.q: To be played that night. It had to be played that night. They didn't have no copy for the Clarenters. You don't remember what job that was. No, that was way from here.

619.s: The elder Sam Dutrey was a great improviser who held his lip like Lorenzo Tio.
619.q: The old man. I'm not talking about his son. I'm talking about the old man. Yeah. Sam, now you're talking about a good improviser. Oh yeah. Oh, he was a great improviser. Great improviser. And Reed too. I never heard him play. He was a good improviser. One of the good of his improvisers as anyone…

191.t: Novelty clarinetists, Tom Gerun's band and Watson's Bellhops
191.s: Kelly recalls double and triple clarinet players, Club Forest in New Orleans in 1932, and Mississippi's Watson's Bellhops brothers.
191.q: Jimmy Maloney of Jimmy George, who played the two clarinets. Yeah. So beautifully together. Played them together and, and, and, real good. And I knew a guy in New Orleans who was with the, uh, Tom Guerin band who played three clarinets at one time.

191.t: Fazola, Sal Franzella and New Orleans clarinetists
191.s: Reed preferences of Fazola, comparison with Sal Franzella, a Mardi Gras parade band and Raymond Burke at the Plantation Club.
191.q: He liked them. He liked them. He, uh, he much preferred the Vandora reeds than anything else. And, uh, when he didn't have, uh, money to buy a box, well, I would pick out the very best reeds in the box for him. And, uh, at that time, uh, Fahs and Sal Franzella were very close. Well, I say friends.…

191.t: Tony Parenti and forgotten New Orleans clarinetists
191.s: Allen credits Tony Parenti with helping start the revival; both note how many clarinetists New Orleans had.
191.q: And particularly in New Orleans, of course, there were just so many of them.

191.t: New Orleans clarinet, trombone and saxophone styles; Eddie Miller
191.s: Kelly says clarinet and trumpet were New Orleans' distinctive instruments and calls Eddie Miller an original stylist.
191.q: And always of the instruments that I think the new audience playing, I think the clarinetist and of course trumpet, trombone, except for good tailgate and good playing, well, of course, Charlie Miller and Julian Lane played well and there were others. But there never was a tromboneist example like…

306.t: Clarinet style he likes: Earl Bostic, Sidney Bechet and a saxophonist named Sport
306.s: Rene praises smooth clarinet and saxophone players and tries with Zander to identify a young man called Sport who came on the riverboat.
306.ch: Uniforms, funeral music and horn styles
306.q: But for me, for the clan that's playing, that suits me. See, my kind of man that's playing there is just like Johnny Bostick, you know. Earl Bostick and them kind of people. Sport and all them kind of people. I'm talking about that other sport that used to come on the boat there.

306.t: Johnny Dodds, Kid Ory and Sidney Bechet as best clarinetist
306.s: Rene remembers Johnny and Baby Dodds in Ory's band and names Bechet the best clarinetist.
306.ch: Joe Rene: Lewis, the Rena band and New Orleans
306.q: Yeah, sure. Sure, he used to play with Ori. I was a kid then. Johnny Dodds, he used to play at the Columny Hall. Johnny Dodds and his baby... Baby Dodds was his brother. He played drum with Ori. Kid Ori's band. I remember that. I used to come around and listen to some fellas, you know.

306.t: Street clarinet players: Willie Humphrey and E-flat clarinets; the Merry-go-round club
306.s: Brass bands had one clarinet; Rene praises Willie Humphrey and mentions small-clarinet types. A recent Merry-go-round club funeral and its dance hall come up.
306.q: They always have one clarinet. We'd have saxophone and things like that. You see Jungle Casualty? Old man Humphrey, and a couple of more. It was one of the best street parade clarinet players you've ever seen. That's Willie Humphrey, the old man.

306.t: Freddie Small, blind clarinetist and memory
306.s: Rene recommends Freddie Small, a blind former Rena player with a good memory, as a source of history.
306.q: Huh? Freddie Small. Yeah. He's a blind fellow. Some kind of preacher, huh? Boy, he could tell you something. He told me some things about myself I didn't know.

859.s: Why Gabriel rates T.O. so high, and Donnell Howard's remark in Chicago.
859.q: So he was playing with Earl Hines, and, because I went there to see George Foster, they were playing in Detroit, so he was telling me, he said, man, I used to look, I used to look at that old tall son, look unfair, that clarinet, and said, God, if I could only play like him, nah, that's what…

859.s: Asked for his favourite clarinetists, Gabriel names T.O. and others like Sam Dutrey, Louis Nelson and Lawrence Dewey.
859.q: Well, I'm going to tell you, that's a hard thing to say because, but I can give you five or six good clarinet players, without putting that temper, I couldn't judge them because that's, I think T.O. was one of the T.O.

859.t: Wade, Johnny Dodds, Georgie Boy and Jimmy Noone
859.s: They discuss Wade's playing, Dodds and Bechet-style players, and Jimmy Newton known as Jimbo.
859.q: Yeah, I know Johnny, he was a routine. I didn't count him. Now when I get to that class, on that kind of class was Sidney Bechet at that time, they all would play like Sidney Bechet, Johnny Dodds, Muley, Muley Bond. Well, they all could jam at that time around the same thing. It was old time, but…

650.t: James McNeil and Charlie McCurtis, who read music upside down
650.s: He praises trumpeter James McNeil as the best musician and Charlie McCurtis, a clarinetist, for reading music upside down.
650.q: Yeah, he could do triple tone. Buddy Bolton. Yeah. He was a cracker jack in that day. And loud, and loud with it. James McNeil was the greatest. James McNeil was the best musician, trumpet player that we ever turned out in New Orleans. I guess you know of him, don't you? James McNeil. He was the…

650.t: Clarinetist Bichet, Arthur Campbell and the many downtown bands
650.s: Bichet played in everyone's band by ear with a gifted tone; Arthur Campbell and Lewis Wade are also praised.
650.q: Yeah, yeah, yeah. He was good too, Arthur Campbell. He had a strange way, a beautiful way of playing, I thought, Arthur Campbell. Lewis Wade, you heard talk of him? Did you hear talk of Lewis Wade? He's a nice player too.

650.t: Clarinet parts, Papa Tio, Piron and Fuclos' dance hall
650.s: Amacker talks about clarinet variations, Lorenzo Tio and his father, Piron and Peter Bocage, and the band he led at George Fuclos' hall on Franklin Street.
650.q: towards the Irish Channel. I'll try to locate him for you if you want. They'll try to locate him for you. Yeah, if you want to cross him. Yeah. You know? Cato and then there. Old timers, old timers. They were very popular in that day. Very popular. Oh, they were very popular in that day. Oh, they…

58.s: They identify a downtown clarinetist as Mealie Barnes, who worked with Buddy Petit.
58.ch: Trumpet styles and early New Orleans scene
58.q: And uh, he played with Rennie and this guy played with Bocard Petit, he's downtown now, way downtown there. That beats me. Yeah, he got a house down there, he don't play much now. You ask Raph about it, Raph took me to his house. Raph knew him good. He lives downtown. Way downtown, yeah.

58.t: Clarinetist Bubba Green and the Amos bands
58.s: Allen asks if Miller knows Bubba Green, who may have played with Amos Riley or Amos White.
58.q: How about knowing if I see him yet? Cause I didn't know anybody in the Amos band but him. He's supposed to play with him. Cause he always had new men to meet my idea. Fellas coming in here from the country, you know.

58.t: Hot and reading clarinet players: George Boyd, Mealy Barnes, Picou
58.s: Miller ranks clarinetists, noting who read and who got off, including George Boyd, Mealy Barnes, Picou and Zeb.
58.q: Well, I don't brag on it, but my boy I had to have me play much clarinet as hot clarinet than anybody I want to hear, George Boyd. He played a whole lot of clarinet. Well, now. Zep was a nice clarinet player, but he didn't play nothing hot. He just, you know. He had to make a hard squeaky note to…

641.t: Fritz's bands and his beautiful tone
641.s: Fritz played with Augustin, Tody Harris and sometimes Toots; his tone was fluid, like Noone and unlike George Lewis.
641.ch: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
641.q: Different style and different tone altogether. I can remember Fritz had a beautiful tone on the clarinet. In fact, he really fascinated me moreso than even Jimmie Noone. But I really believed he played better. The guy was one of these guys that he didn't realize how good he was -- to me.

641.t: Fritz's technique and why George Lewis raved about him
641.s: Fritz was wiry and quiet, with technique and tone Joe admired alongside Jimmie Noone, and Joe could hear it even as a child.
641.ch: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
641.q: He was a kind of wiry looking guy. I would say he was a guy who would remind you of Pops Foster, the bass player. Very quiet. And they had another good clarinet player in Baton Rouge whose name was Green; I can't think of his first name.

641.t: Whether Joe is a New Orleans clarinet player
641.s: Asked about critics who say he is not a New Orleans clarinetist, Joe notes his teachers and influence Fritz, and that many so-called New Orleans players came from elsewhere.
641.ch: Baton Rouge heroes: Guy Kelly and Buddy Petit
641.q: Heh-heh. I don't know. The only thing I could say... The only thing I ever heard when I was a kid was New Orleans clarinet playing, and I took lessons from them. Was Picou a New Orleans clarinet player? What can you say? Maybe I didn't pick up that style exactly. One thing I can say is that I never…

917.t: George Baquet and the clarinet funeral style
917.s: George Baquet played funerals with Manuel Perez's brass band; comparison with Piron and Alphonse Picou; Bechet sleeping in the market.
917.ch: New Orleans clarinetists and learning the guitar
917.q: George Barquet. Yeah, I played with him. George was a good clarinet player, too. And he is a player of funerals. And he was a funer man. He didn't miss a lick. He was right there on the job. Well, I tell you, if I am mistaken, I believe he was a better musician. Not in the line of musician, but in…

917.t: George Baquet's death and his father
917.s: Visiting Baquet sick at home on his return from Chicago and at his wake; Old Man Baquet taught his sons clarinet.
917.ch: New Orleans clarinetists and learning the guitar
917.q: Well, George, when I noticed, I went to his house on Roman, between right, on Roman, between Beville and Abbeville. Of course, I can't say Custom House because he was in Chicago. But I met his wife. And he come home from Chicago and I met his wife over there. There was about the 200 block of Bright…

174.t: Paul Moyer and the clarinet player who took his horn apart
174.s: Dejan sorts out the Moyers: old man Moyer's son took his clarinet apart piece by piece while playing; Paul played drums and Oynice was the clarinetist.
174.ch: Dance jobs and the opera house
174.q: Paul Moyer. Paul was a drummer, huh? He was a fellow that played with Paul Moyer. No, played with an old man Moyer. That's his son I'm talking about. Paul was a drummer.

174.t: Playing with George Boyd at the Willow Inn
174.s: He played with George Boyd at the Willow Inn, where John Casimir would sub on clarinet.
174.q: know a lot about George Boyd and Zeb because I used to play with George Boyd at the Willow Inn. Me, George Boyd, Udell, Willie Dennis Boyd, and when George Boyd couldn't come he used to send John Casper. Well back in that time John was. John John started to play clarinet jack. He was playing for…

246.t: George Stewart, the clarinetist who worked with all the bands
246.s: Glass says George Stewart was slim like George Lewis and worked in the Camellia, Excelsior and any band picking the best men for parades.
246.q: Well he used to work with all the bands, you know. He'd work in with the Camellia Band, Excelsior, he'd work anywhere. You see that's the way they'd hire the fellas, all in between. It's like how all the fellas, they know how all that's good, they'd get him. You see you have to pick out your best…

246.t: Clarinetists, the Tios and Dr. Tudry's family; old man Cottrell

I said Kenny Davern — and we worked together — and I said just bring your clarinet and you, I’ll bring all the recordings, whatever you want to do, and I’ll pay you as much as you…

743.t: Influences, Adele Girard and the harp record
743.s: Gordon cites Pee Wee Russell and Marsala, and loved playing with Adele Girard's jazz harp; a recording from her comeback is played.
743.q: I was highly influenced by Pee Wee Russell quite a bit. I always enjoyed his playing. And the type of playing that I really like to do myself is I used to work with Joe Marsala’s wife, Adele Girard. She was a great jazz harpist. She was the first swing harpist to come along in the 1900s. Casper…

696.t: Baquet great uncles: George and Theo Baquet
696.s: His mother's family, the Baquets, included clarinetist George Baquet and Theo Baquet, who went to New York in 1919.
696.q: was Baquet which is a French name — B-A-Q-U-E-T — George Baquet was a very famous clarinet player who played in the twenties and the thirties, in fact he was one of the teachers of a great saxophone player and a clarinet player from New Orleans called Sidney Bechet. So my great uncle.

585.s: Monk says Davern first gave him her name; she subbed with Greg Cohen on Davern's last gigs, praising his sound, space, and demanding encouragement.
585.q: We did a lot of gigs though, before he passed. You know I was subbing for I’m trying to name the bass player that he played with, Greg —

354.t: The New York Jazz Repertory name and Kenny Davern
354.s: Anecdotes on Davern's humor, strong opinions and unique sound and time.
354.q: Yeah. “The Jazz Repertory.” Kenny Davern gave them a new — you know, N-Y-J-R, the New York Jazz Repertory. And the minute Kenny saw those initials, he says “The New York Jewish Rowing Club.”

116.t: UNO graduate program, Loyola degree and Michael White's influences
116.s: The graduate degree structure and his Loyola experience. He also cannot recall the old clarinetist Michael White studied with.
116.q: It was a liberal arts degree, because the program was under the College of Liberal Arts, but it was – I don’t remember if it was an M.M. They may have used the M.M.E., because it wasn’t a department. It wasn’t a jazz department. The music department was under the purview of the College of Liberal…

80.t: Rudy Powell's Benny Goodman imitation ruins his embouchure
80.s: Rudy tried Goodman's growl, developed a whistle in his tone that spoiled Victor sides, and was replaced by Sedric.
80.q: And he wouldn't have asked for the world, because he was tickled to death to be in the band, and he was playing damned good, and the only thing ruined him then, hurt him, I would put it, he was wrapped up in -- uh -- Benny Goodman playing.

4.t: Slocum Mitchell's clarinet style and its influence
4.s: Slocum Mitchell from Martinique made wailing sounds on clarinet that Spikes says Armstrong and King Oliver later picked up; he never recorded.
4.ch: San Francisco, the So Different Orchestra and Johnny
4.q: No, no, none of us recorded in those days, you know. So, and, uh...he was doing all that stuff... A lot of people nearly trip over when they pass the bandstand sometime, and he'd be playing [vocally imitates Slocum's instrumental style]-- you know, making all that jazz stuff and everything, and…

146.t: Clarinet heroes: Jesse Hooker and Jimmie Noone
146.s: Asked about Johnny Dodds and Jimmie Noone, Smith says Texas clarinetist Jesse Hooker was his real model and he followed him around.
146.ch: Opening and early years in Dallas
146.q: : Jimmie Noone was all right. I didn't get to meet him. But Jesse Hooker, I hung around... I used to follow him around. I'd go up and listen to his band before we went up there and play behind them, when... They were often working around here and play (?) house in the daylight, and I'd follow him…

28.t: Big Boy Goudie, the New Orleans reedman
28.s: Big Boy Goudie (Francis Goudie) played clarinet, tenor and trumpet and led the band the jammers played in; a born jazzman from New Orleans.
28.ch: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
28.q: Oh, yes, sure I knew him well. Sure. Because I used to go down there and jam too. Big Boy, I think he had the band and Big Boy was in the band, and that's --

758.s: Roy praises clarinetist Prince Robinson, who played the Albert system.
758.ch: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
758.q: : And you know who was a helluva musician and a helluva clarinet player, he never really got any recognition in later years, was Prince Robinson.

70.t: Prince Robinson and Ed Inge on clarinet
70.s: Prince Robinson played the clarinet solos on McKinney's early records; Ed Inge played a very modern clarinet, years ahead, and could arrange.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Yeah. He was a fantastic clarinet player and a good tenor player back in those days. He was with McKinney Cottonpickers.

147.t: Buster Bailey, the fastest clarinetist from Memphis
147.s: Crawford praises Buster Bailey, who played with W. C. Handy, as the greatest clarinetist, better than Benny Goodman.
147.ch: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
147.q: And another fellow I was very, very much engrossed in, which I figured was the fastest clarinetist in the world, that was a homey -- hometowner by the name of Buster Bailey. You see, his father disallowed him to play with any other band other than W. C. Handy's. He was the original St. Louis Blues…

384.t: Roger Wolf Kahn, the rich kid who sat in
384.s: Kline asks about clarinetist Roger Wolf Kahn sitting in with Rollini's group, even playing under the table to hide from his parents; Morehouse barely recalls.
384.ch: Studio recordings of the late twenties and thirties
384.q: You know it's too bad that I couldn't have Paul Mertz here. They're coming to see me.

412.t: Rod Cless and the greatness of Johnny Dodds
412.s: Hodes praises clarinetist Rod Cless, who learned from Johnny Dodds, and explains Dodds's three-part New Orleans clarinet style. He says critics do not hear Dodds in context.
412.ch: Wingy Manone and Bix in Chicago (draft typing)
412.q: Yes, Rod Cless on clarinet. And Rod and I -- again, did you know that Rod Cless had been married to Bud Freeman's sister? This I did know, and I think they had a child and they broke up. And, yes, Rod played clarinet with us and he was one of the great clarinet players because, again, the…

115.t: How he came to the World's Greatest Jazz Band; Ed Hall
115.s: Dance asks how Gus joined the band, he recalls the Black clarinettist, Ed Hall.
115.ch: World's Greatest Jazz Band and Denver
115.q: No, no, I didn't. They had a clarinet player before -- what's his name? He died.

455.t: Writing for Ina Ray Hutton and Boyd Raeburn; Jimmy Noone's influence
455.s: Budd and Dizzy write for Ina Ray Hutton and Raeburn, and Budd says Benny Goodman's clarinet sound derives from Jimmy Noone, for whom Budd wrote.
455.ch: Arranging career and the JPJ Quartet
455.q: So with Ina Rae Hutton, I forget what I used to write for her, but I used to -- Dizzy Gillespie was writing for WHEN Boyd Ina Rae, I was writing for Ina Rae, she would come in. Board Rabin, Dizzy Gillespie, Tad Damon and myself, we were --and I don't want to forget this guy's name, I'll recall it…

171.t: Buster Smith as alto and clarinet soloist
171.s: Buster had a soft alto sound, and outplayed Benny Goodman on clarinet.
171.ch: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
171.q: He was a great improviser. He didn't have the strong sound of Hodges or Bird or Benny Carter, like that. He had a soft alto sound, but he was very good as a lead instrument.

79.t: Esque Douglas and the Virginia Ravens
79.s: Esque Douglas, an upperclassman clarinetist, worked with the Virginia Ravens, which also had Eddie Mallory and possibly Doc Cheatham.
79.q: Yes, a tremendous band. A fellow by the name of Eddie Mallory played in that band. And I think Doc Cheatham (?) played in that band but I'm not too sure.
